The bit nobody looks at

It keeps coming back
and nobody can tell you why.

You've had it looked at. It got better. Six weeks later it was back. That's not your physio failing. They fixed the injury properly. It's that nobody asked the other question.

What gets treated

The injury

The tissue, the joint, the thing that hurts. Physios and chiros are genuinely good at this, and you should keep seeing them. But treating the injury doesn't change whatever keeps producing it.

What I work on

Why it keeps coming back

How you move under load. How you breathe when you're tired. Whether your system ever properly recovers, or just carries yesterday into today. Different failure, different question.

You're not training too hard. Your recovery can't keep up.
The Tucker Method

Look. Fix. Then teach.

Three phases. Measured at the start, measured again at the end, so you're never guessing whether it worked.

01
Decompress
Take the pressure off

Assessment and hands-on work. I find what your body is actually doing under load and release what it's been carrying. This is the session where most men feel something change in the room.

02
Restore
Get the breathing working

Breathing retrained as a skill you can run on command, not a reflex you hope holds. Measured: how fast your heart settles, how you breathe when you're tired, how long before panic sets in.

03
Rebuild
Put load back on

Load returns to a body that can handle it now. You leave knowing what your own signals mean, which is the difference between fixing it once and never needing me again.

If it can be measured, it can be changed.
Fit

Who this is actually for.

This is you

  • The same injury has come back more than twice
  • You're fit, and you still gas out under pressure
  • You train hard and wake up feeling like you didn't sleep
  • Fighters who look sharp in the room and lose it under lights
  • You've been told to rest, and resting didn't fix it

This isn't

  • An acute injury that happened this week. See a physio first
  • Anyone after a diagnosis. I don't diagnose and I don't treat conditions
  • Someone looking for a relaxing hour
  • Blokes who want it done to them rather than taught to them

The Guide

I’ve literally been
in the red corner

My first MMA fight lasted sixteen seconds. I lost. The video of it has been watched more than 2.8 million times.

That’s me walking in, before I knew what was coming. I know what it costs to step in under pressure, and what it takes to walk back in after losing in front of everyone. That’s the corner I work from.
